lines.text: Earns 6% a year on shareholders' money

lines.text: Profit per share growing 2% a year

valuation.text: Price tag: in line with its close peers (after adjusting for ROE)

lenses.sp: Wants a large, steady, cheap company with a strong balance sheet.
lenses.vd: In Benjamin Graham's spirit: would probably pass (1 checks use fewer years than the rule needs).

ch.r: Market value above ₹5,000 crore
ch.w: Graham avoided small companies; ₹5,000 crore is our Indian translation of 'adequate size'.

ch.r: Current assets ÷ current liabilities ≥ 2
ch.w: Doesn't apply: banks and finance companies don't split their balance sheet into current and non-current.

ch.r: Long-term debt ≤ current assets − current liabilities
ch.w: Doesn't apply: borrowing is the raw material of a lender's business.

ch.n: A profit every year for 10 years
ch.r: Positive earnings in each of the last 10 years
ch.w: A loss year already breaks this rule, whatever the other years show.

ch.r: Dividends every year for 20 years (India: 10 years)
ch.w: No dividend on record in the last 10 years.

ch.n: Earnings per share up a third in 10 years
ch.r: EPS +33% over 10 years (3-year averages at each end)
ch.w: EPS (average of the first 2 vs last 2 years we have) moved -108%.

ch.r: PE ≤ 15 on 3-year average earnings
ch.w: You pay ₹21 for every ₹1 of average yearly profit over the last 3 yrs.
You pay ₹0.91 for every ₹1 of net worth.

ch.r: Price < √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share)
ch.w: With EPS ₹19.4 and book value ₹182 per share, Graham's ceiling price is ₹282.

lenses.st: Wonderful business at a fair price

lenses.vd: In Warren Buffett's spirit: would probably pass.

ch.r: A lasting edge: brand, low cost, network or switching costs
q: Why can't a well-funded rival copy it?
Has it kept high returns through bad years?

ch.r: ROE ≥ 15% in at least 8 of the last 10 years
ch.w: More than 2 weak years already.

ch.r: No loss in 10 years
ch.w: A loss year breaks the rule.

ch.n: Doesn't eat its cash in capex
ch.r: Capex < 50% of operating cash flow (5-year sum)
ch.w: Doesn't apply to lenders: their 'capex' is lending, which shows up in operating cash flow.

ch.r: Share count up no more than 5% over the years we have
ch.w: Your slice of the company hasn't been shrunk by new share issues.

ch.r: Candid, sensible with capital, no governance red flags

ch.w: Our automatic checks are a starting point only.

lenses.vd: In Charlie Munger's spirit: would probably pass (1 checks use fewer years than the rule needs).

ch.r: PEG (PE ÷ EPS growth) below 2

ch.r: Promoters own ≥ 25% and have pledged none

v4.ll: Passes Kedia-style checks; fails Graham, Buffett, Munger, F-score, Agrawal, Mukherjea-style checks
ch: Leaves Avoid only if the quality score rises above 50 (now 44).
Only 2 valuation methods could be calculated: no Buy or Trim until at least 3 agree on a value.

Any new serious red flag (auditor resigns mid-term, pledge above 25%, SEBI order, negative net worth, weak cash conversion together with high accruals, distress with interest cover below 1.5×) moves it straight to Avoid.

va.pw: Banks and NBFCs: justified P/B and dividends (their cash-flow family), plus own and peer P/B.

dcf.w: Not used for lenders: their cash flow is mostly loans going out and deposits coming in.

epv.w: Not used for lenders (interest is their cost of goods, so EBIT doesn't mean the same thing).

jpb.w: The calculation gives zero or a negative value, so it can't price the share.

ddm.w: Pays no regular dividend, so a dividend model can't value it.

peer_ev_ebitda.w: Not used for financial companies (debt is their raw material).

peer_ev_sales.w: Not used for financial companies (debt is their raw material).

mid_ev_ebitda.w: Needs EBITDA margins and sector EV/EBITDA.

sotp.w: Needs segment / listed-stake data (Stage 5 Company Reader); holding-company discount 20–40% (PROXY) will apply.

nav.w: Needs land bank / investment values from annual reports (Stage 5).

replacement.w: Needs capacity (tonnes) and today's cost per tonne from investor presentations (Stage 5).
